name: Charles' law
seoDesc: Charles' law: work out initial temperature (T₁) from the initial volume and the final volume. A free physics calculator with the formula, units and a…
summary: Supply the initial volume, the final volume, the final temperature and amount of gas and the Charles' law calculator solves for initial temperature (T₁). It is built for a lab report, a problem set or a sanity check on a physical situation. The unit chips sit next to the boxes, which is where most hand-calculation mistakes start.

sections.title: How does the Charles' law calculator work?
sections.html:
The Charles' law calculator takes the values in the form, applies the relationship described below and reports initial temperature (T₁) in the results panel.

Working from the top of the form: you type in the initial volume (V₁), the final volume (V₂), the final temperature (T₂) and amount of gas (n).

Press Calculate and the page works through the equation with the values you supplied and derives the rest; it then keeps up with you as you correct a typo.

Because the equation can be rearranged for each of its variables, the page also runs backwards. Leave the box you want to know empty, fill in the rest, and it solves for the missing one instead. That is useful when you know the answer you need rather than the inputs you have.

sections.title: The formula behind the Charles' law calculator
sections.html:
The page rests on a handful of relationships. Each one can be rearranged for any of its variables, which is what makes the calculator work in both directions:

Initial temperature (T₁)=final temperature (T₂) × initial volume (V₁) ÷ final volume (V₂)
Pressure (p)=(41572299 ÷ 5000000) × amount of gas (n) × initial temperature (T₁) ÷ initial volume (V₁)

Read it as an ordinary equation. Where a word appears instead of a letter, it is the label of one of the boxes in the form; where a function appears, it is the usual mathematical meaning of that function.

sections.title: What is a worked example?
sections.html:
Suppose Initial volume (V₁) = 10 m³, Final volume (V₂) = 10 m³ and Final temperature (T₂) = 10 K. Working through the relationship above gives Initial temperature (T₁) = 10 K.

Read it as a template. Every number above can be replaced with one of yours; only the relationship between them is fixed.

  1. Enter the values listed above, matching the units each box asks for.
  2. Read off the result. Any field you leave empty is the one the calculator solves for.
  3. Sanity-check the number against the relationship: Initial temperature (T₁) = 10 K should be roughly the size you expected from Initial volume (V₁) = 10 m³ and Final volume (V₂) = 10 m³.

If a number looks wrong, check three things in this order: that the units match what you had in mind, that no drop-down is still on its default, and that the value you entered is on the same scale as the rest — a rate typed as 5 rather than 0.05 is the classic mistake. Those three account for almost every answer that is out by a factor.

sections.title: How are units and precision handled?
sections.html:
Every quantity with units carries a chip beside its box. Switching the chip does not change what you know, only how it is written: values are converted to a common internal base, the arithmetic happens there, and the answer is converted back for display. Mixing metres with feet in one calculation is therefore safe.

  • Volume, opening in cubic meters
  • Temperature, opening in kelvins
  • Volume, opening in cubic meters
  • Temperature, opening in kelvins
  • Pressure, opening in pascals
  • Mole, opening in moles

Results are rounded for display but computed at full precision, so chaining one result into the next does not accumulate error. Very large and very small numbers switch to scientific notation rather than printing a run of zeros.

sections.title: When should you use it?
sections.html:
The Charles' law calculator earns its place in the middle of a task, not instead of one. It is most useful when:

  • Solving a problem set where the algebra is more interesting than the arithmetic
  • Writing up a lab result and needing a quick cross-check
  • Testing whether an answer is physically plausible before you trust it
  • Any time the same 4 figures keep coming back — the initial volume, the final volume and the final temperature — and you would rather not repeat the arithmetic by hand each time.

sections.title: How do you get a reliable answer?
sections.html:
• If a result surprises you, look at the order of magnitude before the digits: a plausible number in the wrong unit looks more convincing than an implausible one, and is easier to miss.
  • Round only at the end. The calculator carries full precision internally, so re-entering a value you already rounded is the fastest way to introduce drift.
  • Compare two scenarios by changing the input that actually differs between them, and keep the rest fixed, so the difference you see is the difference you meant to test.
  • Change one input at a time when you are exploring. Two simultaneous changes make it impossible to tell which one moved the result.

sections.title: What else is worth knowing?
sections.html:
• Filling in more than one box is fine. The most recently edited field is the one treated as known, so you can switch direction without reloading.
  • Fields that are still blank are exactly the ones the calculator has not yet been given, so the results panel is a reliable map of what is missing.

faq.q: What does the Charles' law calculator work out?
faq.a: It returns initial temperature (T₁), derived from the initial volume, the final volume and the final temperature. Every field in the form feeds the same relationship: press Calculate once and changing any of them updates the result immediately, with no page reload.

faq.q: What do I need to enter to use the Charles' law calculator?
faq.a: The form asks for the initial volume, the final volume, the final temperature and amount of gas, which is 4 fields in total. Each one is labelled with what it means and, where relevant, the unit it expects. Anything you leave blank is treated as the value to solve for.

faq.q: Can I enter initial volume (V₁) in a different unit?
faq.a: Yes. Initial volume (V₁) opens in cubic meters and the chip beside it offers 40 units. The number you typed keeps its magnitude and only its label changes; the calculation itself happens in a common base unit, so mixing systems in one form is safe.
Yes. Each variable in the relationship can be the one being solved for: fill in the answer you are aiming at, leave the field you want empty, and the calculator inverts the equation for you.

With the values the page starts from, the calculator reports Initial temperature (T₁) = 10 K. Treat that as a reference point rather than a recommendation: it exists so you can tell at a glance whether your own inputs are on the same scale.

faq.q: Is the Charles' law calculator free to use?
faq.a: Yes — no account, no sign-up and no limit on how many times you run it. The arithmetic happens in your browser, so the values you type are not sent anywhere.
